entries.clue: S American footballers damage animals' home - again! (6,4)

blocks.note: SA is the standing short form for South American
the FA is the Football Association, which runs the game in England
to rip a thing is to tear it, one way of damaging it
Noah's vessel took two of every creature aboard
the setter owning up that three of his words are wanted twice, once for their letters and once for their meaning

annotation.surface: South American footballers wrecking a zoo, and not for the first time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Again' is the confession: the last piece of the wordplay means what the definition means, so those three letters are earned twice over. The trap is reading 'S American footballers' as a team rather than two short forms stacked.
annotation.definitionFit: A safari park is a drive-through reserve where the animals roam loose and the visitors stay in the car, so it houses them as much as any ark did.

entries.clue: Pipsqueak, second with attitude (4)

blocks.note: s is the clock's abbreviation for a second
lip is backchat: giving someone lip is answering back

annotation.surface: A little nobody who came second and still has plenty to say.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads as a placing and means a unit of time. A slip of a lad or a slip of a girl is standing English for someone slight and young, and it is the only place the sense survives.
annotation.definitionFit: A slip of a lad is a slight, undersized one, which is the size calling somebody a pipsqueak cuts them down to.

entries.clue: Oscar wearing fleece, a square (4)

indicatorNotes.wearing: What you wear goes round the outside of you, so the fleece is written round the letter that has put it on.

blocks.note: a fleece is an animal's own coat, so the word stands for fur
Oscar is O in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: Oscar in a fleece, which is not a good look.
annotation.walkthrough: The square in the sentence is the unfashionable sort of person; the square wanted is the arithmetic kind, a number multiplied by itself. Fleece here is the sheep's coat rather than the verb meaning to swindle.
annotation.definitionFit: Four is two times two, so it is a square number — a square in the mathematician's sense rather than a shape with corners.

entries.clue: Predecessor redeployed, prepared for new task (11)

indicatorNotes.redeployed: Redeploying sends people to new positions, and letters sent to new positions are no longer standing where they were.

blocks.note: eleven letters to work from, exactly the length wanted
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The person who had the job before you, posted elsewhere and readied for something new.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the clue's first word with nothing marking it off, which is where a long anagram hides best. 'Prepared for new task' is said of material rather than of people, and the sentence wants you reading about a colleague.
annotation.definitionFit: Material that has been reprocessed has been put through the works a second time and made ready for a use other than its first.

entries.clue: Spanish bread, once risen: gorge before 30 days (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Bread is slang for money and stays singular however much of it there is, while the answer is a countable plural — the coins and notes themselves.

indicatorNotes.risen: In a down entry the letters are written from the top downwards, so a piece that has risen is read from its foot back to its head.

blocks.note: to gorge yourself is to sate your appetite
sep is the diary's short form of September, the month the old rhyme gives thirty days

annotation.surface: Spanish loaves that have proved, and a blow-out before a month of going without.
annotation.walkthrough: Bread is slang for money, and 'once' does the dating: the currency wanted is the one the euro replaced in 2002. The whole assembly is read upwards, not merely its last piece.
annotation.definitionFit: The peseta was Spain's money until the euro came in, so 'Spanish bread, once' is cash that country spent and no longer does.

entries.clue: Overcome bottle (7)

blocks.note: what you do to a difficulty when you settle it for good
British slang for nerve: somebody who backs out has lost theirs

annotation.surface: Getting the better of the drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves are different parts of speech — a verb for settling a difficulty, a noun for nerve — which is why two words side by side do not read as one phrase. To bottle it is to lose your nerve.
annotation.definitionFit: To resolve a problem is to overcome it, and resolve the noun is the steadiness under pressure that British slang calls bottle.

entries.clue: Ask many questions where real ale delivered (4)

blocks.note: keep at somebody for information and you are working a handle up and down
the tall lever on a pub bar that draws cask beer up from the cellar

annotation.surface: Quizzing somebody hard about where the good beer is served.
annotation.walkthrough: Real ale is cask beer, hauled up by hand from the cellar rather than pushed up by gas, which is why a British bar has a row of levers along it. Pumping a person for news borrows the same handle.
annotation.definitionFit: To pump somebody is to keep drawing information out of them, and the beer engine on the bar is what draws cask ale up into the glass.

entries.clue: Hollywood superstar I don't know hurt a bad guy (3,7)

indicatorNotes.bad: Something gone bad has not kept its shape, and letters that have not kept their shape are letters out of their order.

blocks.note: the noise you make while failing to come up with an answer
five letters to rearrange, the clue's own two words
a guy is a man

annotation.surface: Some film star you cannot name laying out a villain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad guy' is the phrase the eye keeps whole, and the clue splits it: 'bad' does the shuffling and 'guy' hands over letters. Uma Thurman took a sword to plenty of bad guys in Kill Bill.
annotation.definitionFit: Uma Thurman headlined Pulp Fiction and both volumes of Kill Bill, which is Hollywood stardom of the first rank.

entries.clue: Invention: what's uncovered when we see headgear? (4-3,3)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: To uncover a thing is to take off what covers it, so the letters at the two ends come away and the middle is what is left.

blocks.note: Cockney rhyming slang for a lie, and an invention is a lie
the three letters at the centre of the word, once its outer two have gone

annotation.surface: A riddle about what a piece of headgear leaves on show.
annotation.walkthrough: Rhyming slang is a London game: pork pies rhymes with lies and wears down to 'porkies' in speech. 'Uncovered' does to the word exactly what taking a hat off does to a head, which is where the joke sits.
annotation.definitionFit: A pork-pie hat is the flat-crowned, narrow-brimmed felt hat named for the pie it resembles — Buster Keaton's, and half of 1960s ska.

entries.clue: Leads on models, love? Sounds plausible (1,7,2)

blocks.note: a side ahead in a game is up: two up with three to play
to model for a painter is to pose
love is a tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

annotation.surface: Somebody after tip-offs about models, and only half believing what they are told.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' is the trap: it is asking whether a thing is plausible, not asking you to say anything out loud. 'Is up' for leads comes off a scoreboard, and its four letters straddle two words of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: 'I suppose so' is what you say when a story is plausible enough to accept and not good enough to endorse.

entries.clue: Declare provision of food 'passably good' ... (4)

indicatorNotes.Declare: To declare something is to say it out loud, and a word said out loud can be written down another way.

blocks.note: the food provided at table is the fare, and that word spoken is the spelling wanted here

annotation.surface: A verdict on the catering: no worse than all right.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots at the end run the sentence into 11 across, which is a separate clue with wordplay of its own. Fare meaning food survives mainly in 'bill of fare', the old name for a menu.
annotation.definitionFit: Work marked fair is passable and no better — the school report's word for adequate.

entries.clue: ... top it all off with rich snack item (8,4)

indicatorNotes.off: Food that has gone off has spoiled, and letters that have gone off do not stay in the order they were served in.

blocks.note: eight of the twelve letters, the clue's own three words
the other four letters, joined on
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Finishing the spread off with something indulgent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top it all off' is so ordinary a phrase that the eye reads straight past it, and it is two thirds of the fodder. The instruction sits inside the phrase it operates on rather than beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A tortilla chip is the fried triangle of corn sold for dipping, which is a snack and nothing else.

entries.clue: Fans, hating a touring country (11)

indicatorNotes.touring: A tour goes round and comes back by another way, so what it carries arrives in an order other than the one it set out in.

blocks.note: eleven letters to work from, the length wanted
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Supporters with no love at all for the side that has come to tour.
annotation.walkthrough: A touring country in cricket is the visiting Test side, which is the picture the sentence paints. 'A touring country' reads as one phrase, and in fact the a belongs to the letters while only the last word defines.
annotation.definitionFit: Afghanistan is the landlocked state between Iran and Pakistan, one country among the many a bare 'country' could be pointing at.

entries.clue: Separate beds for Rosemary and Basil? (4,6)

annotation.definition: Separate beds for Rosemary and Basil?

blocks.note: read as a couple who have stopped sharing a bedroom, and meant as the dug plots a gardener plants one crop to
two first names on the surface, and two plants on the windowsill of every British kitchen

annotation.surface: A couple called Rosemary and Basil who no longer share a bedroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Capital letters are free in a cryptic — a setter may capitalise anything — and both of these names are plants before they are people. A bed is the gardener's word for a dug plot, and herbs are commonly given one each.
annotation.definitionFit: A herb garden is laid out in separate plots so that rosemary and basil do not run into one another, which is the clue read as plants.

entries.clue: After Mexican beer, one put into empty taco new way of serving chicken (10)

indicatorNotes.After: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the beer leads off and everything else follows it.
indicatorNotes.empty: An empty word has had its insides taken out and keeps only the letters at its two ends.
indicatorNotes.put into: Something put into a thing ends up within it, so the single letter goes between the two that are left.

blocks.note: Corona is the pale lager brewed in Mexico and drunk with a wedge of lime
the word's first and last letters, with the two in the middle gone
the Roman numeral for one
n is the standard short form for new

annotation.surface: A new chicken recipe that starts with a Mexican beer and a barely filled taco.
annotation.walkthrough: Coronation chicken is British catering's standby cold dish — mayonnaise, curry powder, apricot — so the definition names a real recipe rather than describing one. 'New' looks like part of that phrase and is a single letter of wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Coronation chicken was invented for Elizabeth II's coronation lunch in 1953, and British menus still name the dish by that one word.

entries.clue: They have run off before the match (7)

annotation.definition: They have run off before the match

blocks.note: read as a side taking to the field, and meant as two people leaving in the night
a fixture on the surface; a match is also a marriage, and this pair did not wait for the one arranged for them

annotation.surface: A team that has left the pitch before kick-off.
annotation.walkthrough: Match for marriage is the older sense — a good match, a matchmaker — and the clue needs it alongside the sporting one. 'Run off' is the standing phrase for leaving with somebody you were not supposed to.
annotation.definitionFit: Elopers are the couple who slip away to marry without anyone's leave, so they have gone before the match their families had in mind.

entries.clue: Everyman's beginning to cycle round garden: watch out (2,5)

indicatorNotes.cycle round: To cycle round is to come back to where you started, so the letters keep their order while the one on the end travels round to the front.

blocks.note: the first letter of the setter's own name
the same six letters in the same order, with the last of them brought round in front

annotation.surface: Everyman setting off on his bike for a lap of the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his puzzles by name, so 'Everyman's beginning' is the setter pointing at his own first letter, a habit of his. The bike in the picture is there to stop you reading 'cycle' as an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: En garde is the fencing call to come on guard before the blades go in, which is a warning to watch out.

entries.clue: Become lovelier - or succeed, showing one's magnificence, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Become lovelier - or succeed, showing one's magnificence, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: What is primary comes first, so every word gives up only the letter it begins with.

blocks.clueFragment: Become lovelier - or succeed, showing one's magnificence
blocks.note: the opening letters of the seven words, taken in the order they are written

annotation.surface: Someone growing better-looking, or getting on and making sure it shows.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the sentence says what the answer means and its initials spell it. Everyman ends an initials clue with 'primarily' most weeks, so the last word is worth reading first.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is what a plant and a person both do: come into flower, come good, and look magnificent doing it.

entries.clue: Fellow, revolutionary was in charge, leader in Africa (7)

annotation.definition: Fellow, revolutionary was in charge, leader in Africa

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: A revolution turns a thing right round, so the piece beside it is read from its last letter back to its first.
indicatorNotes.leader in: The leader in a word is the letter at its head, and no more of it than that.

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
whoever was in charge led, and that word is turned round here
the letter the continent's name starts with

annotation.surface: A man of revolutionary views who once ran the country, somewhere in Africa.
annotation.walkthrough: No word is spare for a definition because the whole sentence is one: the man, the revolutionary, the head of state. Nelson Mandela led the armed wing of the ANC, spent 27 years in jail and came out to become South Africa's president.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is Mandela's life: a revolutionary who ended up in charge and remains the African leader of the century.

entries.clue: Performing, fall apart: neither piano nor forte and I can't remember the words (3-2-2)

indicatorNotes.Performing: A piece performed is played rather than read off the page as written, and letters played are letters that come out in another order.

blocks.note: nine letters to work from, two more than are wanted
in a score p marks piano and f forte, and a passage that is neither loses both letters

annotation.surface: A singer coming to pieces on stage, neither soft nor loud and fluffing the lyrics.
annotation.walkthrough: Piano and forte are italicised because they are the score's own words, and a score prints them as single letters. 'Fall apart' is both the picture of the performance and the pile the two letters come out of.
annotation.definitionFit: Tra-la-la is the nonsense a singer falls back on when the words have gone, filler that keeps the tune moving.

entries.clue: By replacing pinch of nutmeg with a little turmeric, what was increasingly unpleasant becomes more savoury (7)

indicatorNotes.replacing: What replaces a thing stands exactly where it stood, so the new letter goes into the gap the old one leaves.
indicatorNotes.pinch of: A pinch is the smallest amount a cook takes, and the smallest amount of a word is the letter it starts with.
indicatorNotes.a little: A little of a word is the start of it, one letter and no further in.

blocks.note: getting worse and worse is getting this, seven letters with one about to be traded
the first letter of that spice, and the one that goes
the first letter of the other spice, taking the vacated place

annotation.surface: A cook swapping one spice for another and improving the dish.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is a recipe instruction doubling as a spelling instruction, with both spices named only for the letters they begin with. 'What was increasingly unpleasant' is a comparative, which is the tip that the word wanted ends in -er.
annotation.definitionFit: Something tastier has more flavour in it than whatever it is being set against, which is what more savoury says.

entries.clue: A group on stage's vacuously trendy? Leaves in a hurry (8,4)

indicatorNotes.vacuously: A vacuous word is an empty one, so all that survives of it is the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
a band is a group of musicians
the clue's own word, taken as it stands
the first and last letters of the word, with everything between them emptied out
hip has meant trendy since the jazz clubs

annotation.surface: A band on stage who are stylish in a thoroughly empty sort of way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A group on stage' is one picture and four separate pieces, which is what makes the front of this hard to break open. The apostrophe-s counts as part of the word, so both ends of 'stage's' are S.
annotation.definitionFit: To abandon ship is to get off fast because the vessel is going down, and the phrase is used of leaving anything that is sinking.

entries.clue: Stand a drop of hollandaise (4)

indicatorNotes.a drop of: A drop of a thing is a small part of it, and the small part wanted is a run of letters inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: four letters in a row, starting six into the sauce's name and stopping one short of its end

annotation.surface: Offering somebody a spoonful of the sauce to see whether they can take it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stand' reads as tolerate in the sentence and means a raised platform in the answer. Hollandaise is the butter-and-egg-yolk sauce, and a word that long is roomy enough to bury something in.
annotation.definitionFit: A dais is the low platform a speaker or a top table is raised on, so it is a stand in the plain sense of a thing stood upon.

entries.clue: Hunk overstudious? Not entirely (4)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: Not entirely means some of it and not all, so a run of letters inside the word is wanted rather than the whole of it.

blocks.note: four letters in a row, starting five into the word

annotation.surface: Denying that the beefcake spends quite all his time with his books.
annotation.walkthrough: The question and its answer are both surface: 'Not entirely' looks like a reply and is an instruction to take only part of the word in front of it. Hunk for a well-built man is American slang that stuck.
annotation.definitionFit: A stud is a man with a reputation built on his looks and his conquests, which is the build calling him a hunk credits him with.

entries.clue: Drop turkey perhaps on the counter (4)

indicatorNotes.on the counter: To counter is to go against, so the word runs against the way the entry is written, its last letter arriving first.

blocks.note: a turkey is one kind of bird, 'perhaps' marking it as an example, and the word is then run the other way

annotation.surface: A turkey left out on the kitchen worktop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' is the kitchen surface in the sentence and an instruction to read right to left in the answer. A drib is the singular behind 'dribs and drabs', which is about the only place the word still turns up.
annotation.definitionFit: A drib is a small drop or driblet of liquid, the sense preserved in 'dribs and drabs' for bits arriving a little at a time.

entries.clue: Main point hidden in concerning tirade: he's on a roll! (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a whole sentence where the answer is a noun: it describes the man on the list, and the answer is what you call him.

indicatorNotes.hidden in: What is hidden in a thing is written inside it, so the piece named first goes in between the letters of what follows.

blocks.note: re is the heading at the top of a memo, meaning concerning
the gist of an argument is its main point
a tirade is a rant

annotation.surface: A furious letter with the real point buried somewhere inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hidden in' is not the hidden-word signal it looks like: nothing runs consecutively through the clue's own letters, and the instruction is to put one piece inside another. The outer piece is itself two words far apart in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A registrant is somebody entered on a register, and roll is the older word for one — the school roll, the electoral roll.

entries.clue: Less than one sister escaping from trap (4)

indicatorNotes.escaping from trap: A trap is a mouth in British slang, so whatever escapes from it is being spoken, and a spoken word may be written another way.

blocks.note: a sister in a convent is a nun, and that word said aloud is spelt as it is here

annotation.surface: Not even one of the convent getting away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trap' for mouth is British slang — shut your trap — and it is what makes this a sound clue rather than a deletion. The two spellings are exact homophones in nearly every English accent.
annotation.definitionFit: None is the count below one: not a single one of whatever was being counted.

entries.clue: Frequented - with scorn? (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition leans on the first: 'frequented with scorn' is the setter's shorthand for the answer's other sense, talking down to somebody.

blocks.note: went back again and again as a customer, which is what a shop's regulars do
the same verb used of somebody talking down to you, kindly on the face of it and insulting underneath

annotation.surface: A shop somebody keeps going back to while looking down their nose at it.
annotation.walkthrough: A patron is both a customer and a protector, and it is the protector sense that soured into condescension. The dash asks for the same verb read twice rather than joining two halves of one sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: To patronise a shop is to frequent it as a customer; to patronise a person is to treat them with the scorn that dresses itself up as kindness.
